sentences: This bill would let the Department of Home Affairs run systems for sharing identity information between governments.
It sets up a hub and a national driver licence facial recognition database, with rules for what can be shared and with whom.
The bill also includes penalties for unauthorized use of information and requires annual reports and a review.
changes: The bill gives the Department of Home Affairs legal authority to collect, use, and share identity information.
It establishes an interoperability hub for data sharing between agencies.
It creates a National Driver Licence Facial Recognition Solution.
It defines the scope of identity-matching services, including their functions and allowed users.
It introduces accountability measures like annual reporting and penalties for unauthorized disclosure.
summary.affected: Commonwealth, state, and territory government agencies, and private sector organizations that use identity-matching services.

speeches.speaker: David Coleman
speeches.brief: The bill amends the Australian Passports Act 2005 to allow the foreign minister to automate sharing of passport data with Commonwealth, state and territory agencies for national security and identity-matching purposes, following a 2017 COAG decision. It aims to enable real-time detection of identity fraud and terrorist threats while maintaining privacy safeguards.

speeches.speaker: David Coleman
speeches.brief: The Identity‑matching Services Bill 2019 was moved to implement the Intergovernmental Agreement on Identity Matching Services, enabling facial‑image sharing for national security, law enforcement, community safety and road safety via a Face Verification Service and a Face Identification Service (banned from live facial recognition and criminal watchlists). The bill includes privacy safeguards, annual parliamentary reporting, and a statutory review within five years; identity crime affects one in four Australians costing over $2 billion annually, and five states have already passed similar legislation.
